thread_name: Phone connection to face to face meeting.
summary_a:
This email thread covers the logistical coordination required to set up a US telephone bridge for remote participants attending an upcoming face-to-face meeting in Amsterdam. Charles McCathieNevile initiated the thread to assess whether team members needed remote access. Several individuals, including William Loughborough, Marjolein Katsma, and Phill Jenkins, confirmed their intent to call in. Phill specifically requested a toll-free 800 number because he would be away from his office. 

The main discussion revolved around managing significant time zone differences, as the scheduled Amsterdam meeting hours of 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM correspond to early morning hours across North America. To accommodate his local Mountain Time schedule, Phill decided he would only join the session during the second half of the day. The group decided to proceed with establishing the US bridge connection based on the demonstrated interest. As an action item, Charles McCathieNevile agreed to follow up early the following week with confirmed schedule details, including the exact post-lunch call-in time for remote attendees.

This email thread addresses the need for a non-technical, plain-language version or primer of the W3C Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG). Alan Cantor initiates the discussion after receiving feedback from an amateur web developer that the current guidelines and Quick Tips are overly technical and difficult to parse. Robert Neff agrees with the idea, emphasizing that a simplified guide would significantly improve user community buy-in and implementation. 

During the discussion, Chuck Letourneau points to existing resources, specifically the WCAG Curriculum and Example Set, noting that these will soon relocate to W3C space for broader promotion. Jonathan Chetwynd advocates using concrete examples rather than heavy text, providing a link to a prototype website, although Judy Brewer subsequently reports server connection issues with those links. 

Ultimately, the group supports the initiative to make accessibility documentation more approachable for non-experts. As a key action item, William Loughborough requests that Alan Cantor take on the task of creating this user-friendly version or primer.

This email thread serves as the initial welcome and introduction for members of the Web Accessibility Initiative Evaluation and Repair Interest Group (WAI-ER-IG). Chair Leonard Kasday initiated the exchange by inviting participants to share their professional backgrounds and experiences related to web accessibility. Responses came from representatives across academia, industry, and advocacy organizations, including W3C, IBM, the Trace Center, and the American Foundation for the Blind. Key discussion points focused on defining the group's advisory role to the Evaluation and Repair Working Group (ER-WG), specifically regarding tools used for evaluating, repairing, and filtering websites. Participants highlighted their plans to gather empirical data, conduct usability testing, and help refine project deliverables. While no formal technical decisions were finalized, the group established its core commitment to support the ER-WG through ongoing brainstorming and prototyping solutions. Action items include individual commitments to actively participate in listserv discussions, attend regular meetings, evaluate tools such as BOBBY, explore content filtering capabilities in platforms like Lotus Notes Domino, and incorporate feedback from webmasters, users with disabilities, and other relevant stakeholders.

thread_name: Appropriate Use of Graphics, and Web Design by Blind People
summary_a: This email thread explores the potential implications of establishing a Priority 1 accessibility requirement to use graphics, specifically concerning how it affects blind web designers and those lacking visual artistic skills. Kynn Bartlett initiates the discussion by questioning whether requiring graphics to aid individuals with cognitive disabilities would unfairly disadvantage blind designers who might struggle to create visual content. Charles McCathieNevile responds that visual capabilities vary individually among both blind and sighted people. Kynn further clarifies that unlike describing existing images, requiring graphics forces authors to generate visual assets, which many designers—sighted or blind—cannot easily do. Jonathan Chetwynd criticizes this perspective, arguing that dismissing specific user needs undermines web accessibility principles. In response, Leonard Kasday highlights that blind designers can successfully utilize rule-based visual tools, such as automated flowchart generators, standardized icon sets, and structured layout templates, to meet functional usability standards without requiring artistic vision. Kynn concludes by addressing Chetwynd’s critique, calling for constructive dialogue rather than personal assumptions. No final decisions were reached and no formal action items were established during this exploratory debate.

This email thread addresses the selection of a map graphic for SWADEurope promotional postcards ahead of the www2003 conference. The visual map will overlay coordinate data showing the locations of Semantic Web researchers and groups. Libby Miller requests immediate feedback on two designer options: a globe graphic showing Europe within the wider world, and a flat map showing Europe in isolation. Both Ian Dickinson and Dan Brickley prefer the flat map over the globe, with Dan highlighting that geographical accuracy simplifies plotting coordinate data. Ian raises concerns about the globe being visually cluttered and the map leaving a large, empty Atlantic area, suggesting a schematic approach instead. Libby notes that the empty ocean space on the map could actually be advantageous for placing project logos or slogans. Ultimately, the group leans toward using the flat map over the globe option. As an action item, Libby will forward this feedback and Ian's design suggestions to the designer to refine the map layout as quickly as possible.

This email thread details the planning and logistical coordination for an upcoming W3C working group face-to-face meeting aimed at resolving document issues and refining techniques following a last call review. Charles McCathieNevile initially proposed holding the two-day meeting in the Boston area on October 7–8. Key discussion points revolved around potential schedule conflicts, such as the concurrent ATIA meeting in Orlando and individual travel obligations raised by group members like Ian Jacobs and Kynn Bartlett. After reviewing the alternatives, a final decision was reached to officially set the meeting for October 7 and 8, hosted by Allaire Corp at the Royal Sonesta Hotel in Boston. Key action items for meeting participants include registering via the provided web link by October 1 and reserving hotel rooms under the group discount by September 10 due to high seasonal demand. Additionally, attendees are required to submit their lunch menu preferences or state any dietary restrictions to Charles by 3:00 PM Boston time on Monday to finalize catering plans.
